findings.who: A filer with self-only HDHP coverage all year who divorced in April 2025 and remarried in October 2025. The first spouse had family HDHP coverage from January through April.
findings.why_no: The computed gate requires the filer to be not married at the end of 2025. Because the filer had remarried by December 31, the gate is false and the question about the former spouse is never asked. The current-spouse branch covers only the spouse at year end, so the earlier spouse's family coverage during the first marriage never reaches the return.
findings.line: f8889.former_spouse_family_if_asked (set to false; the refusal it leads to is missed, and line 3 uses self-only $4,300 for months that count as family)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan. Disregard any plans with self-only coverage"; p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who ... had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"
findings.fix: Drop 'not married at the end of 2025' from the gate. Ask every filer with self-only coverage all year whether any marriage that ended during 2025 (before a remarriage or not) involved a spouse with family HDHP coverage in a month of that marriage.

findings.who: A recently divorced filer whose former spouse had employer coverage for the spouse and the children. The filer does not know whether that plan was a high-deductible plan, or does not remember its type.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether the other person had 'a high-deductible plan covering more than one person.' The filer cannot check the plan's HDHP status for an ex-spouse and defaults to no. The help explains 'covering more than one person' but never says how to tell whether a plan was high-deductible.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan"
findings.fix: First ask a fact the filer can check: did the then-spouse have any health plan covering more than one person, or have or receive contributions to an HSA? Then add help on how to recognize an HDHP, for example a plan the spouse paired with an HSA, or one with a high deductible stated in the plan papers. Treat 'not sure' as yes (refusal).

findings.who: A filer with self-only HDHP coverage all twelve months who was married until mid-2025 to a spouse with family HDHP coverage. The filer was not an eligible individual in one or more months, for example after enrolling in Medicare or because of a spouse's general-purpose health FSA during the marriage.
findings.why_no: The 'self_only' branch also requires the filer to be 'an eligible individual in every month.' When that fails, the computed gate is false and the former spouse's family coverage is never asked about. That coverage still sets family treatment for the eligible months of the marriage in the Line 3 monthly worksheet.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules"; p. 4, Line 3 rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage"
findings.fix: Confirm that a filer who was ineligible in some month is refused or routed to a path that asks about the then-spouse's family coverage month by month. If neither happens, widen the gate to cover self-only filers who were eligible in only some months.

locators: p. 4, How To Complete Part I, "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan"

p. 4, How To Complete Part I, "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan. Disregard any plans with self-only coverage"; p. 7, Line 6, "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules to figure the amount on line 6"
p. 4, How To Complete Part I; p. 7, Line 6

findings.who: A filer moved IRA money into the HSA in February 2024 as a qualified HSA funding distribution, lost HDHP coverage in May 2024, and so failed that testing period and reported it on the 2024 return. They regained HDHP coverage before December 1, 2024 and used the last-month rule to contribute the full 2024 amount. They then lost HDHP coverage again in mid-2025.
findings.why_no: The computed gate is false whenever the testing period of a 2024 qualified HSA funding distribution 'has already been failed'. The last-month-rule question is then never asked, although the two testing periods are separate and the last-month rule's runs from December 1, 2024 to December 31, 2025.
findings.line: f8889.testing_prior_if_asked (feeds Form 8889 Part III line 18 for 2025)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 9, Part III: 'failure to be an eligible individual during the testing period for: • Last-month rule ..., or • A qualified HSA funding distribution'; p. 2: 'If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period ... you will have to include in income the total contributions made that would not have been made except for the last-month rule.'
findings.fix: Do not suppress the last-month-rule question because a funding distribution's testing period was failed. At most, suppress it only when the funding distribution's failure fell in the same months and the instructions state that one inclusion replaces the other. Otherwise compute line 18 independently of line 19.

findings.who: A filer used the last-month rule for 2024 and also contributed for 2025. They had no HDHP from March to October 2025, then regained it before December 1, 2025 and used the last-month rule again for 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate is asked only if the filer was 'not an eligible individual in every month of 2025'. If the 2025 monthly eligibility comes from 'are, or are considered, eligible', the 2025 last-month rule treats them as eligible for all of 2025. The gate then reads as passed, although they actually failed the 2024 testing period in March 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2: 'The testing period begins with the last month of your tax year and ends on the last day of the 12th month following that month ... If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period ... you will have to include in income the total contributions made that would not have been made except for the last-month rule.'
findings.fix: Base the gate on actual first-of-month eligibility in each month of 2025, ignoring any 2025 last-month-rule treatment. Alternatively, ask directly: 'Was there any month in 2025 when, on the first day, you or your spouse lacked HDHP coverage, had other health coverage, were enrolled in Medicare, or were someone's dependent?'

findings.who: On a joint return, only the spouse has an HSA. The spouse used the last-month rule for 2024 and lost eligibility in 2025, while the filer contributed for 2025 and was eligible all year.
findings.why_no: If the 'contributions for 2025' and 'eligible in every month of 2025' facts are taken once per return, or for the primary filer only, the spouse's 2024 testing period is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4: 'If married filing jointly and both you and your spouse have HSAs, complete a separate Form 8889 for each of you.'
findings.fix: Evaluate the gate and its inputs separately for each HSA account beneficiary, naming the spouse in every 2025 contribution and eligibility question.

locators: p. 2, Last-month rule, "You may consider yourself an "eligible individual" for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year"; p. 2, Testing period, "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include in income the total contributions made that would not have been made except for the last-month rule"; p. 4, Line 3, rule 2, "You are treated as having the same HDHP coverage for the entire year as you had on the first day of the last month of your tax year"; p. 9, Part III
p. 2, Testing period; p. 8, Testing period; p. 9, Part III
p. 2, Testing period; p. 9, Part III

findings.who: A married filer had self-only HDHP coverage and was HSA-eligible from March 1 through December, with no HDHP in January or February. The spouse, also eligible, had family HDHP coverage (spouse and child) all year.
findings.why_no: The computed gate is false because the filer did not have self-only coverage on the first day of every month and was not eligible in every month. The spouse's family coverage is never asked, and the gated line is set to false.
findings.line: f8889.spouse_family_if_asked (and through it line 3 and the Line 3 Limitation Chart months, which use self-only instead of family)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, Line 3 rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage. Disregard any plan with self-only coverage." How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan."
findings.fix: Ask the spouse-family question of every married filer who was an eligible individual in any month of 2025, not only one with self-only coverage every month. Apply the answer month by month in the Line 3 chart.

findings.who: A married filer first became eligible with self-only HDHP coverage on December 1 (or mid-year) and uses the last-month rule. The spouse was eligible with family HDHP coverage on December 1.
findings.why_no: The filer was not eligible in every month and lacked coverage on the first day of every month, so the gate computes false. The question about the spouse's family coverage is never reached.
findings.line: f8889.spouse_family_if_asked (line 3 under the last-month rule gives $4,300 instead of $8,550)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, Line 3 rule 2: "If the last-month rule ... applies, you are considered an eligible individual for the entire year. You are treated as having the same HDHP coverage for the entire year as you had on the first day of the last month"; Line 1: "If you and your spouse are considered covered by a family HDHP, you are considered covered by a family HDHP regardless of whether you file jointly or separately."
findings.fix: Ask the spouse-family question whenever the filer is married at year end and was eligible on December 1 or in any month. Determine December 1 coverage type after applying the spouse rule.

findings.who: A married filer is eligible with self-only HDHP coverage all year. The spouse has no HSA and is on an employer or marketplace bronze plan covering the spouse and children. The plan is HSA-qualified but is never called a "high-deductible plan" in the spouse's materials.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether the spouse had "a high-deductible plan." A spouse without an HSA often does not know the plan is an HDHP, and the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, Line 3 rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage."
findings.fix: Ask a fact the filer can check: "In any month of 2025, was your spouse on a health plan covering more than one person (for example, spouse and child) that their employer or insurer describes as HSA-eligible or HSA-qualified, or that has a deductible of at least the family HDHP minimum?" Add help explaining how to check plan documents or the Summary of Benefits.

locators: p. 4, How To Complete Part I, "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan"

p. 4, How To Complete Part I, "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan. Disregard any plans with self-only coverage"; p. 4, Line 3, rule 1, "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage"
p. 4, Line 3, rule 1, "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage"

findings.who: A filer with HSA contributions for 2025 who moved IRA money into the HSA in, say, September 2024, and who kept the high deductible plan all of 2025 but lost eligibility for another reason (enrolled in Medicare mid-2025, became covered by a spouse's general-purpose health FSA, or became claimable as a dependent).
findings.why_no: The gate closes only on the computed helper 'Not an eligible individual on the first day of at least one month of 2025', whose month questions are not shown here. If those questions ask about HDHP coverage rather than every eligibility condition, this filer reports HDHP coverage in all twelve months, the helper is false, and the 2024 IRA question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Testing period: 'If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual. This amount is also subject to a 10% additional tax.'
findings.fix: Confirm the monthly helper tests full eligibility (HDHP coverage, no disqualifying other coverage, not enrolled in Medicare, not claimable as a dependent), not just HDHP coverage. Otherwise ask the 2024 IRA transfer question of everyone with an HSA, since it is a fact the filer can check.

findings.who: A joint return where the filer was eligible in every month of 2025 and had contributions, but the spouse received an IRA-to-HSA transfer in 2024 and dropped HDHP coverage during 2025.
findings.why_no: The gated question is per person ('you, or your spouse on a joint return'), but the gate description does not say whether the contributions and monthly eligibility helpers are also computed per person. If they use only the primary filer's answers, the gate is false for the spouse and the spouse's question is skipped.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 9, Part III: 'Use Part III to figure any additional income ... for failure to be an eligible individual during the testing period for ... A qualified HSA funding distribution'; Line 19: 'Enter the total of any qualified HSA funding distribution (see line 10).'
findings.fix: State and verify that the gate is evaluated separately for each spouse's own Form 8889, using that spouse's contributions and that spouse's monthly eligibility.

findings.who: A filer who reaches the gated question and whose IRA custodian, in 2024, issued a check payable to the HSA trustee that the filer delivered, or who thinks of the event as a 'rollover' or 'one-time funding distribution'.
findings.why_no: The words 'straight from an IRA' and the help 'The IRA's custodian sends the money directly to the HSA. Money you took out of an IRA and deposited yourself does not count' can be read to exclude a transfer the filer physically carried. The question also does not say that both traditional and Roth IRAs count.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Testing period: 'If you received a traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution, you must remain an eligible individual during the testing period. The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA'
findings.fix: Reword to: 'In 2024, was money moved from a traditional or Roth IRA to your HSA as a one-time trustee-to-trustee funding transfer (a qualified HSA funding distribution)? Answer yes even if the check was made out to the HSA trustee and you delivered it.'

locators: p. 1, Who Must File, "You failed to be an “eligible individual” during a “testing period” and must recognize income"; p. 9, Part III

p. 8, Testing period, "If you received a traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution, you must remain an eligible individual during the testing period. The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA and lasts through the last day of the 12th month following that month"; p. 9, Part III
p. 8, Testing period; p. 9, Part III

findings.who: A filer whose HDHP did not run as one type for all twelve months (started a job with HDHP coverage on February 1, or moved from self-only to family on marrying in June), and who, or whose spouse, had a general-purpose health FSA or HRA in 2025. Examples: a spouse's ordinary health FSA at work from the wedding onward, or a 2024 FSA with money left whose grace period ran into March 2025.
findings.why_no: They truthfully pick 'anything else (including coverage that started, ended or changed type)'. The gate is then the constant false, the FSA/HRA question is never asked, and the line is treated as false (no FSA). Nothing shown here says the month-by-month path asks about an FSA, and filers do not see an FSA, least of all a spouse's, as 'other health coverage'.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 5: 'An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA.' and 'Coverage during a grace period by a general purpose health FSA is allowed if the balance in the health FSA at the end of its prior-year plan is zero.' i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'You must be, or be considered, an eligible individual on the first day of a month to take an HSA deduction for that month.'
findings.fix: Ask the FSA/HRA question of everyone with any HDHP month, not only when coverage was uniform and the three conditions held all year. On a yes, ask which months the FSA or HRA (including a grace period with a balance) covered either spouse. Treat those months as not eligible in the Line 3 worksheet, and deny the last-month rule if December 1 is covered.

findings.who: A filer with self-only or family HDHP coverage in all twelve months who truthfully says the three conditions did not hold every month for a reason unrelated to an FSA (enrolled in Medicare from October, or on a parent's non-HDHP plan through March). They or their spouse also had a general-purpose health FSA or HRA during the months they believe were eligible.
findings.why_no: The three-conditions answer is a truthful no because of Medicare or the other plan. That no closes the gate, so the FSA question is skipped and the line is false. The remaining months are counted as eligible although the FSA or HRA disqualifies them too.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'you must be covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP) and have no other health coverage except certain disregarded coverage.' p969 (2025) p. 5: 'An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA.'
findings.fix: Take the FSA/HRA question out from under the three-conditions gate and ask it whenever there is any HDHP month. Alternatively, when the three conditions fail, ask month by month and name a health FSA or HRA of either spouse (and a grace-period balance) in that question as coverage that makes a month ineligible.

findings.who: A filer with uniform HDHP coverage who is enrolled in their own or a spouse's general-purpose health FSA or HRA and knows, or is told by the three-conditions wording, that it might count as 'other health coverage that is not disregarded'. They answer the three-conditions question no for that reason.
findings.why_no: The three-conditions question comes before the FSA question, and its own wording already covers the FSA, so a careful filer answers no there. The gate closes and the tool records no FSA. It then treats the year as a month-by-month case with no record of why, so the FSA-specific rules (limited-purpose, post-deductible, grace period with zero balance, suspended HRA) are never applied. The filer may be refused or cut down although the arrangement is a permitted one, or may be counted as eligible in the months they report.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 5: 'However, an employee can make contributions to an HSA while covered under an HDHP and one or more of the following arrangements. Limited-purpose health FSA or HRA... Suspended HRA... Post-deductible health FSA or HRA... Retiree-only HRA.'
findings.fix: Ask the concrete FSA/HRA question first, or independently of the three-conditions question. Word the three-conditions question to say 'apart from any health FSA or HRA, which is asked about separately'.

locators: p. 2, Eligible Individual; p. 4, Line 3, rule 3 (a year that was not the same in every month is counted month by month)
p. 5, Other employee health plans

p. 5, Other employee health plans, "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA" and the four arrangements that follow (limited-purpose health FSA or HRA, suspended HRA, post-deductible health FSA or HRA, retiree-only HRA)

findings.who: A married filer who had their own self-only HDHP on the first day of all twelve months and was eligible all year, while the spouse, also eligible, had an HDHP covering the spouse and the children (family coverage) all year.
findings.why_no: The first helper asks about 'HDHP coverage on the first day of every month of 2025: self-only in all twelve', and the filer's own plan was truthfully self-only in all twelve. The next helper, 'self-only all year as an eligible individual', is also true. The only text that says a spouse's plan covering more than one person makes this person 'family' is the help on the December 1 question, which is never shown.
findings.line: f8889.dec_coverage_if_changed (set to year_self_only, so line 3 uses $4,300 instead of $8,550, and the line 1 box is wrong)
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3 rule 1: 'Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage. Disregard any plan with self-only coverage.' Also How To Complete Part I: 'if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan.'
findings.fix: In the first helper, ask about the coverage the person had or is treated as having. State there: 'If you were married and either spouse had an HSA-qualifying plan covering more than one person while you both qualified, answer family for those months.' Alternatively, ask on a joint or married-separate return whether the spouse had a family HDHP at any time in 2025 and route to family or changed accordingly.

findings.who: A filer with their own self-only HDHP in all twelve months who married during 2025, or whose spouse started a family HDHP mid-year (for example in October), so that on December 1 both were eligible and the spouse had family coverage.
findings.why_no: Their own plan never 'started, ended or changed type'. It was self-only on the first day of every month, so they truthfully pick 'self-only in all twelve' and the coverage is never classed as 'changed'.
findings.line: f8889.dec_coverage_if_changed (December 1 coverage is taken as self-only, so the rule 4(b) amount of $8,550 is lost and the month-by-month chart is not used either)
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3 rule 4(b): 'The maximum amount that can be contributed based on the type of HDHP coverage you had on the first day of the last month of your tax year', with the TIP: 'If you had family coverage on the first day of the last month, you do not need to use the worksheet; enter $8,550 on line 3.'
findings.fix: Add to the 'anything else' option: 'or your spouse's family HDHP started or ended during the year, or you married or divorced during the year'. Ask the December 1 question whenever the filer was married at any time in 2025 and the spouse had any HDHP.

findings.who: A filer with their own self-only HDHP all year who was also covered all year, or for part of it, as a dependent child under 26 or domestic partner on someone else's family HDHP.
findings.why_no: They read the question as being about their own plan and pick 'self-only in all twelve'. Having two plans at once is not obviously coverage that 'started, ended or changed type'. The rule that both kinds at once counts as family appears only in the hidden December 1 help.
findings.line: f8889.dec_coverage_if_changed (self-only instead of family, so line 3 is too low)
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 1: 'If you were covered by both a self-only HDHP and a family HDHP at the same time, you are treated as having family coverage during that period.'
findings.fix: Move the rule into the gate helper: 'Count yourself as family for any month you were on any HSA-qualifying plan covering more than one person, including someone else's plan, even if you also had a self-only plan.'

findings.who: A filer with the same HDHP on the first day of all twelve months who enrolled in Medicare (often retroactively at 65), was covered by a spouse's general-purpose health FSA or other non-HDHP coverage, or could be claimed as a dependent, in December or for part of the year.
findings.why_no: The second helper turns on the legal term 'eligible individual'. A filer who kept the HDHP all year reads 'self-only all year as an eligible individual' as true. The plain-language list of what makes December 1 'none' (Medicare, other coverage that pays medical bills, dependent status) is help text on the question that is never asked.
findings.line: f8889.dec_coverage_if_changed (taken as self-only or family when it should be none, so line 3 gets the full-year limit instead of the month-by-month worksheet amount or zero)
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3 rule 5: 'If you were not an eligible individual on the first day of the last month of your tax year, use the Line 3 Limitation Chart and Worksheet'. Also Figuring Your HSA Deduction: 'You cannot deduct any contributions for any month in which you were enrolled in Medicare. Also, you cannot deduct contributions if you are someone else's dependent for 2025.'
findings.fix: Replace 'as an eligible individual' with facts the filer can check, asked before the all-year shortcut: 'In any month of 2025 were you enrolled in Medicare (including backdated Part A), covered by any other health plan or a general-purpose FSA or HRA, or able to be claimed as a dependent?' Any yes routes to 'changed' and the December 1 question.

findings.who: A filer whose HDHP covered themselves and one other person (employee plus child or employee plus spouse) all year, and who does not think of a two-person plan as 'family'.
findings.why_no: The gate offers only 'self-only' or 'family' without defining them. The definition 'a plan covering more than one person' appears only in the help of the gated December 1 question, so the filer picks self-only.
findings.line: f8889.dec_coverage_if_changed (self-only instead of family, so line 3 is $4,300 instead of $8,550)
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Figuring Your HSA Deduction: 'If you have self-only coverage, your maximum contribution is $4,300. If you have family coverage, your maximum contribution is $8,550.'
findings.fix: Define the terms in the gate helper: 'self-only means the plan covered only you; family means it covered you and at least one other person (including employee plus one).'

findings.who: A fiscal-year individual filer whose tax year does not end in December.
findings.why_no: The gate and the question both hard-code 'every month of 2025' and 'December 1, 2025'. The filer answers for calendar months, although the test date is the first day of the last month of their own tax year.
findings.line: f8889.dec_coverage_if_changed (coverage taken on the wrong date)
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 1: 'on the first day of the last month of your tax year (December 1 for most taxpayers)'
findings.fix: Word both as 'the first day of the last month of your tax year (December 1 for calendar-year filers)' and 'every month of your tax year', or refuse fiscal-year filers explicitly.

locators: p. 4, How To Complete Part I, Line 1 ("If you were covered by both a self-only HDHP and a family HDHP at the same time, you are treated as having family coverage during that period") and Line 3 rules 1, 2 and 4(b), spouse-attributed family coverage and the coverage on the first day of the last month

p. 4, Line 3, rule 3, "If you were, or were considered, an eligible individual for the entire year and you did not change your type of coverage, enter $4,300 for a self-only HDHP or $8,550 for a family HDHP on line 3"; p. 4, Line 3, rules 4 and 5
p. 4, Line 3, rules 2, 3 and 4(b) (the coverage on the first day of the last month, and under rule 3 an eligible individual for the entire year who did not change the type of coverage)

findings.who: A filer with family HDHP coverage on the first of every month who, for part of the year, also had a self-only HDHP. Or a filer covered as a member of a spouse's or parent's family HDHP for January to June, then by their own family HDHP for July to December.
findings.why_no: The help says that if they were covered as a member of someone else's plan, or by a self-only and a family plan at once, they choose 'covering more than one person', and 'if that was so for only part of the year, choose “No”.' Their overlap or membership lasted only part of the year, so they choose No. But the coverage counted as family coverage in every month, so the type never changed.
findings.line: f8889.clear_if_uniform (set to false; clear_all_year never asked)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, Line 1: "If you were covered by both a self-only HDHP and a family HDHP at the same time, you are treated as having family coverage during that period"; Line 3, rule 3: "eligible individual for the entire year and you did not change your type of coverage, enter ... $8,550 for a family HDHP"
findings.fix: Replace the 'part of the year' sentence. Tell the filer to choose 'covering more than one person' if, on the first of every month, they were on at least one plan covering more than one person, whether their own or someone else's, even if the plans changed during the year. Choose No only if some first-of-month had no HDHP or only a self-only HDHP.

findings.who: A filer whose HDHP stayed a family plan all year but whose tier changed. Examples: they moved from 'employee + child' to 'employee + spouse' or 'family' at marriage, or a child left the plan while a spouse stayed on.
findings.why_no: They read the tier change as a change in the 'kind' of plan. The help says only that a change of insurer with no gap is not a change.
findings.irs_text: p969 p. 4: "Family HDHP coverage is HDHP coverage for an eligible individual and at least one other individual (whether or not that individual is an eligible individual)"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Only two kinds count: only you, or you and at least one other person. Changing among tiers such as employee+spouse, employee+children or family, or adding or dropping family members, is not a change as long as at least one other person was covered.'

findings.who: A filer who changed jobs, moved to COBRA continuation, or renewed into a new plan year mid-year, with no gap and an HDHP of the same tier throughout.
findings.why_no: The help names only 'a change of insurer' as not a change. A new employer plan, COBRA, or a new plan year can read as a different plan, so the filer answers No to 'the same kind all year'.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, Line 3, rule 3: "If you were ... an eligible individual for the entire year and you did not change your type of coverage, enter $4,300 for a self-only HDHP or $8,550 for a family HDHP"
findings.fix: Say: 'A change of insurer, employer, plan, or plan year, or a move to COBRA, with no gap and the same coverage tier is not a change.'

findings.who: A filer whose plan meets the HDHP deductible and out-of-pocket limits, such as a self-only plan with a $1,700 deductible, but whose papers never say 'HSA-eligible' or 'HDHP', or who has no HSA through the employer.
findings.why_no: They don't see the label or an employer HSA, so they read 'works with an HSA' as not met. A $1,700 deductible may also not seem 'high'.
findings.irs_text: p969 p. 4: minimum annual deductible for 2025 "$1,650" self-only and "$3,300" family; maximum annual deductible and other out-of-pocket expenses "$8,300" and "$16,600"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'If your papers don't say, check the 2025 limits: a deductible of at least $1,650 for only you or $3,300 for more than one person, and out-of-pocket costs no more than $8,300 or $16,600.' State that you need not have an HSA through your employer.

locators: p. 2, Eligible Individual, "you must be covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP) and have no other health coverage except certain disregarded coverage ... You must be, or be considered, an eligible individual on the first day of a month"; p. 4, Line 1, "If you were covered by both a self-only HDHP and a family HDHP at the same time, you are treated as having family coverage during that period"; p. 4, Line 3, rule 3, "If you were, or were considered, an eligible individual for the entire year and you did not change your type of coverage, enter $4,300 for a self-only HDHP or $8,550 for a family HDHP on line 3"; , "Family HDHP coverage is HDHP coverage for an eligible individual and at least one other individual"

p. 2, Eligible Individual, "you must be covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP) and have no other health coverage except certain disregarded coverage ... you cannot be enrolled in Medicare or be another person's dependent"; p. 2, Certain coverage disregarded and Permitted insurance; p. 2, Eligible Individual, VA hospital care or medical services for a service-connected disability and benefits under surprise billing laws; p. 4, "You cannot deduct any contributions for any month in which you were enrolled in Medicare. Also, you cannot deduct contributions if you are someone else's dependent for 2025"; , Enrolled in Medicare, "This rule applies to periods of retroactive Medicare coverage"
p. 2, Eligible Individual; p. 4, Line 3, rule 3 (a year that was not the same in every month is counted month by month)

used.how: pages named by another document's citation

findings.who: A fiscal-year individual filer whose tax year does not end in December. They had no HDHP on December 1, 2025 but were an eligible individual on the first day of the last month of their own tax year.
findings.why_no: The question fixes the date as 'December 1, 2025', and on that date they truthfully had no coverage, so they answer 'none'.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'if you are an eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year (December 1, for most individuals)'; p. 4 Line 3 rule 2: 'the first day of the last month of your tax year'
findings.fix: Ask about 'the first day of the last month of your tax year (December 1, 2025 for calendar-year filers)', or ask the tax year end first and compute the date. Otherwise refuse fiscal-year returns explicitly.

findings.who: A return for a decedent who died before December 2025 (for example in August) and who became HDHP-covered mid-year and was an eligible individual on the first day of the month of death. The short tax year ends at death.
findings.why_no: The preparer or surviving spouse answers 'none' for December 1, 2025 because the person was no longer alive or covered then.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year (December 1, for most individuals)'; Testing period: 'other than because of death or becoming disabled'
findings.fix: For a decedent's return, ask about coverage on the first day of the month of death (the last month of the tax year). Otherwise state a refusal for decedent returns with part-year HSA eligibility.

findings.who: A spouse on a joint return (or a non-dependent adult child or domestic partner) who on December 1 was covered only as a family member under someone else's family HDHP, having joined that plan mid-year. They hold no policy in their own name.
findings.why_no: They read 'HDHP coverage you had' as a plan they themselves enrolled in or hold, and answer 'none' because the plan is the spouse's or parent's.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4 Line 1: 'If you and your spouse are considered covered by a family HDHP, you are considered covered by a family HDHP'; Line 3 rule 1: 'Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage'
findings.fix: Word it as 'On December 1, 2025, was this person covered by an HSA-qualifying plan, whether their own or as a family member on a spouse's, parent's or anyone else's plan?' Say that coverage under another person's family plan counts as family coverage.

findings.who: A filer who started an HDHP mid-year and on December 1 also had dental, vision, telehealth, accident, disability, specified-disease or hospital-indemnity insurance, or received VA care for a service-connected disability.
findings.why_no: The upstream helper is framed as 'coverage as an eligible individual'. Believing the other coverage or VA care disqualifies them, they answer 'none' for 'had or were treated as having'.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'Certain coverage disregarded. An eligible individual may have... Coverage for accidents, disability, dental care, vision care, long-term care, or telehealth'; 'does not fail to be treated as an eligible individual... merely because the individual receives hospital care or medical services under any law administered by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs for a service-connected disability'
findings.fix: Add help text saying that dental, vision, telehealth, accident, disability, long-term care and permitted insurance, and VA care for a service-connected disability, do not stop you being eligible. Tell the filer to answer by the HDHP they had on the date.

findings.who: A filer who enrolled late in 2025 in an employer or marketplace plan sold as 'HSA-eligible' or 'consumer-directed'. They do not know it is an 'HDHP' or what 'treated as having' means.
findings.why_no: 'HDHP' is a legal classification and 'treated as having' is undefined. Unsure, they pick 'none', or they picked a non-HDHP answer at the upstream coverage helper.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'you must be covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP)'; 'You may consider yourself an "eligible individual" for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year'
findings.fix: Ask a checkable fact: 'On December 1, 2025, were you covered by a health plan that lets you contribute to an HSA (often labelled HSA-eligible or high deductible)? Did it cover only you, or you and at least one other person?' Explain 'treated as having' with the spouse family-coverage rule.

findings.who: A filer first covered by an HDHP late in 2025 (for example from November 1 or December 1) with no HDHP earlier in the year.
findings.why_no: The upstream choices are 'self-only all year, family all year, or changed during the year'. Their coverage type never 'changed', it only began, so no option fits. If they exit through a 'not covered' or 'none' path they never reach the December 1 or last-month question.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: 'You may consider yourself an "eligible individual" for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year'; p. 4 Line 3 rule 2
findings.fix: Relabel the third option 'covered for only part of the year, or the type of coverage changed'. Always ask the December 1 coverage for anyone not covered the same way in all 12 months.

locators: p. 2, Last-month rule and Testing period; p. 4, Line 3, rule 2
p. 2, Last-month rule, "for the entire year if you are an eligible individual"; p. 4, Line 3, rule 2
p. 4, Line 3, rules 2, 3 and 4(b) (the coverage on the first day of the last month, and under rule 3 an eligible individual for the entire year who did not change the type of coverage)

findings.who: A nonspouse beneficiary (for example an adult child) who inherited an HSA from an owner who died in 2025 but took no money out until 2026. Likewise the final 2025 return of a deceased owner whose estate is the beneficiary and where nothing was paid out during 2025.
findings.why_no: Line 14a asks for 'Total distributions you received in 2025 from all HSAs'. Nothing was paid out in 2025 and no 2025 Form 1099-SA exists, so 14a is truthfully 0 and the computed gate is false.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa p. 3, Nonspouse beneficiary: 'you must report as income on your tax return the FMV of the account as of the date of death. Report the FMV on your tax return for the year the account owner died even if you received the distribution from the account in a later year.' Estate beneficiary: 'the fair market value (FMV) of the account on the date of death is includible in the account holder's gross income. Report the amount on the account holder's final income tax return.'
findings.fix: Do not gate the death question on line 14a > 0. Ask everyone with any HSA connection: 'Did you (or your spouse) inherit an HSA in 2025 from someone who was not your spouse, or is this a final return for an HSA owner who died in 2025 with the estate as beneficiary — even if no money has come out yet?' Route a yes to the death-distribution handling or refusal.

findings.who: An HSA owner who never withdrew cash but paid with the HSA debit card or had the trustee pay providers directly. Some of that spending was not qualified (premiums, an adult child who is not a dependent, costs from before the HSA was opened, or costs later reimbursed by insurance).
findings.why_no: They read 'distributions you received' as money paid to them, so they enter 0 on line 14a. The gate is then false and the medical-use question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa p. 3, Box 1: 'Shows the amount received this year. The amount may have been a direct payment to the medical service provider or distributed to you.' i8889 p. 2: 'Any part of a distribution not used to pay qualified medical expenses is includible in gross income and is subject to an additional 20% tax unless an exception applies.'
findings.fix: Word the 14a input as: 'Total money that came out of your HSAs in 2025 by any route — debit card purchases, payments sent straight to a doctor or pharmacy, transfers or checks to you, rollovers, and excess contributions taken back (Form 1099-SA box 1)'.

findings.who: An HSA owner who engaged in a prohibited transaction or pledged the HSA as security for a loan in 2025. The account is treated as distributed, but no cash left it.
findings.why_no: They 'received' nothing, so they enter 0 on line 14a, particularly if the Form 1099-SA is late or missing. The gate is false and the box 3 code question that would catch code 5 is never asked.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa p. 3, Box 3: '5—Prohibited transaction'. i8889 p. 8, Line 14a: 'Enter the total distributions your HSAs made in 2025. These amounts should be shown on Form 1099-SA, box 1.'
findings.fix: Make the gate 'line 14a > 0 OR any 2025 Form 1099-SA for an HSA was received OR the account was used as loan security or in a prohibited transaction'. Add help on 14a: 'Include amounts treated as distributed even if no cash came out.'

findings.who: A filer who took HSA money out in 2025 but has no Form 1099-SA in hand (lost, sent to an old address, or account closed), or whose spouse's separate HSA made the distributions on a joint return.
findings.why_no: Line 14a is tied to 'Form 1099-SA, box 1', so with no form they enter 0. A 'you' reading can also omit the spouse's HSA if the 14a input is not clearly asked once for each spouse.
findings.irs_text: f8889 p. 1, Part II: 'If you are filing jointly and both you and your spouse each have separate HSAs, complete a separate Part II for each spouse.' f1099sa p. 3: 'File Form 8853 or Form 8889 with your Form 1040 or 1040-SR to report a distribution from these accounts even if the distribution isn't taxable.'
findings.fix: State on the 14a input: 'Enter the amount even if you did not get a Form 1099-SA', and ask it separately for each spouse's HSAs on a joint return.

locators: p. 1, Part II, "HSA Distributions", "Total distributions you received in 2025 from all HSAs" (line 14a)

p. 3, Instructions for Recipient, "Box 3. These codes identify the distribution you received: 1—Normal distribution; 2—Excess contributions; 3—Disability; 4—Death distribution other than code 6; 5—Prohibited transaction; 6—Death distribution after year of death to a nonspouse beneficiary"
p. 3, Instructions for Recipient, Box 1 and Box 3

p. 2, Distributions From an HSA, "Distributions from an HSA used exclusively to pay qualified medical expenses of the account beneficiary, spouse, or dependents are excludable from gross income"; p. 8, Line 15, "Only include on line 15 distributions from your HSA that were used to pay you for qualified medical expenses not reimbursed by insurance or other coverage and that you incurred after the HSA was established"
p. 8, Line 15

findings.who: The executor or surviving spouse files the final return of an HSA owner who died in 2025, alone or jointly with the surviving spouse. The HSA had no designated beneficiary, or named the estate, so the estate is the beneficiary.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'you' got an HSA or money from one 'because its owner died'. For the decedent, the person was the owner and got nothing. The estate took the account, so no for either spouse is truthful.
findings.line: f8889.inherited_case_if_any (it defaults to inh_spouse_earlier, which refuses nothing; the date-of-death value that belongs on the final return is dropped or the case is not refused)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: 'If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return. Complete Form 8889 as described above, except you should complete Part I, if applicable.'
findings.fix: Add a second gate question for each person: 'Did this person die in 2025 owning an HSA that went to their estate, or had no named beneficiary?' Route a yes into the 'anything else' case.

findings.who: A child was named beneficiary of a parent's HSA, and the parent died in 2025. At filing time the trustee had not yet paid out or retitled the account, for example because the claim paperwork was still pending.
findings.why_no: 'Did you get an HSA, or money from one' reads as receipt. Nothing has been received yet, so they answer no. Yet the account stopped being an HSA at death, and its date-of-death value is the beneficiary's to report.
findings.line: f8889.inherited_case_if_any (it defaults to inh_spouse_earlier instead of the 2025 nonspouse case, so the refusal or amount is missed)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: 'If the designated beneficiary is not the account beneficiary's surviving spouse, or there is no designated beneficiary, the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death... On Part II, line 14a, enter the fair market value of the HSA as of the date of death.'
findings.fix: Ask about the fact, not receipt: 'Were you named as beneficiary of, or are you entitled to, an HSA whose owner died, even if you have not received anything yet?'

findings.who: A surviving spouse's husband or wife died in 2025. The trustee retitled the HSA in the survivor's name, or moved it into the survivor's existing HSA by trustee-to-trustee transfer.
findings.why_no: They think of the account as their own HSA now, not as something they 'got' or money paid to them. The help that says a spouse's HSA 'now counts as your own' appears only after a yes. So they answer no, and the year of death falls into the default 'death before 2025' case.
findings.line: f8889.inherited_case_if_any (it takes inh_spouse_earlier, the death before 2025, when the 2025 death belongs in 'anything else', so the refusal is missed)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: 'If the account beneficiary's surviving spouse is the designated beneficiary, the HSA is treated as if the surviving spouse were the account beneficiary.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help: 'Answer Yes even if the account was moved or retitled into your name, or merged into your own HSA.'

findings.who: A filer was named beneficiary by a sibling, friend, or unmarried partner, or a trust named them, and the owner died in 2025.
findings.why_no: The help's examples, 'a parent, or a husband or wife', can be read as the full list of relationships that count.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 1: 'You acquired an interest in an HSA because of the death of the account beneficiary.'
findings.fix: Change the help to 'anyone — for example a parent, a husband or wife, a sibling, or a friend — named you…'

locators: p. 1, Who Must File, "You acquired an interest in an HSA because of the death of the account beneficiary"; p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary
p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary

p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary, "If the account beneficiary's surviving spouse is the designated beneficiary, the HSA is treated as if the surviving spouse were the account beneficiary. The surviving spouse completes Form 8889 as though the HSA belonged to the surviving spouse." and "If the designated beneficiary is not the account beneficiary's surviving spouse, or there is no designated beneficiary, the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death"

findings.who: A filer turned 65 in 2024 and moved a qualified HSA funding distribution from an IRA in September 2024. In mid-2025 they applied for Social Security, and Medicare Part A was made retroactive for up to 6 months, into early 2025. When answering the 2025 month-by-month coverage questions, they reported HDHP coverage in every month.
findings.why_no: The 2025 answers say HDHP coverage every month, so the tool computes 'eligible individual in every month of 2025' and never asks the 2024 funding distribution question. The filer still had the HDHP and does not think of retroactive Part A as Medicare enrollment in those months.
findings.line: f8889.ira_gap_if_prior (and through it Form 8889 line 19, plus the 10% additional tax)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: 'If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period ... you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual. This amount is also subject to a 10% additional tax.'
findings.fix: Base the gate on each disqualifying fact for each month of 2025, not only on HDHP coverage: Medicare enrollment (including Part A made retroactive), other non-HDHP coverage, and being claimable as a dependent. Or ask the 2024 funding distribution question whenever any 2025 HSA activity exists, and let the testing-period question resolve it.

findings.who: A filer with HDHP coverage made a 2024 funding distribution. In 2025, their spouse elected a general-purpose health FSA that could reimburse the filer's expenses, or the filer was covered by a spouse's non-HDHP plan as secondary coverage. They reported HDHP coverage in every month of 2025.
findings.why_no: The 2025 month answers ask about the HDHP the filer had, so the computed condition shows eligible every month. The filer does not see the spouse's FSA or secondary plan as 'other health coverage that pays medical bills.' The gate never surfaces the testing-period question.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: 'you must remain an eligible individual during the testing period'; p. 9 Part III: 'Line 19 Enter the total of any qualified HSA funding distribution.'
findings.fix: Make the 2025 eligibility answers that feed this gate name disqualifying coverage explicitly, such as a spouse's general-purpose health FSA or HRA, or secondary non-HDHP coverage. Or do not let 'HDHP every month' alone suppress the 2024 question.

findings.who: On a joint return, the spouse made the 2024 funding distribution into the spouse's own HSA. The spouse lost eligibility in March 2025. The primary filer was eligible all year.
findings.why_no: If the gate's eligibility test or the 'contributed to your HSA in 2024' question is evaluated only for the primary filer, the filer answers no ('your HSA') or the computed condition is satisfied by the filer's months. The spouse's failure is never asked.
findings.line: f8889.ira_gap_if_prior for the spouse (spouse's Form 8889 line 19)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: 'If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period ... you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income'
findings.fix: State that the gate is evaluated separately for each spouse, using that spouse's own 2025 months. Word the question as 'to your HSA (or, on a joint return, to your spouse's HSA, asked separately)'.

findings.who: In 2024, a filer had a Roth IRA custodian transfer money directly to their HSA, which was their once-in-a-lifetime transfer.
findings.why_no: The filer may read 'qualified HSA funding distribution from an IRA' as covering traditional IRAs only, or may not recognize the term for a custodian-to-custodian transfer.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: 'If you received a traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution, you must remain an eligible individual during the testing period.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2024, did you move money directly from any IRA (traditional or Roth) into your HSA?'

locators: p. 8, Testing period

p. 8, Testing period, "The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA and lasts through the last day of the 12th month following that month. For example, if the distribution is contributed on June 17, 2025, the testing period lasts through June 30, 2026."
p. 8, Testing period; p. 9, Part III

findings.who: A non-spouse designated beneficiary (for example, an adult child) inherited a parent's HSA when the parent died in 2025. Within a year of the death, the beneficiary paid the parent's final hospital and doctor bills.
findings.why_no: The list of 'Whose costs count' names only 'yours, and your spouse's', dependents, would-be dependents, and children of separated parents. A deceased parent who was not the filer's dependent is none of these. Read truthfully, the list makes the filer exclude the decedent's bills and report zero or too little.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary: 'On Part II, line 15, for a beneficiary other than the estate, enter qualified medical expenses incurred by the account beneficiary before the date of death that the beneficiary paid within 1 year after the date of death.'
findings.fix: Ask first whether the HSA was inherited from someone other than a spouse. If yes, ask separately for the decedent's medical expenses incurred before death that the beneficiary paid within 1 year after the death, and put that amount on line 15.

findings.who: The same non-spouse beneficiary. The parent died in late 2025 and the beneficiary paid the parent's last medical bills in early 2026, within the one-year window, before filing the 2025 return.
findings.why_no: The gate is framed as 2025 distributions 'used to pay' expenses, and the question asks how much of 'the money that came out paid for' costs. Payments made in 2026 do not fit that 2025 framing, and the cost-date rule 'after you opened the HSA' does not describe the decedent's case.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: 'qualified medical expenses incurred by the account beneficiary before the date of death that the beneficiary paid within 1 year after the date of death.'
findings.fix: For an inherited non-spouse HSA, state that payments made up to 1 year after the date of death count, even if they were made after 2025.

findings.who: The filer (or the spouse) inherited a parent's HSA in 2025 as a non-spouse beneficiary and withdrew nothing. The account simply passed to them, and a Form 1099-SA reports its value at the date of death.
findings.why_no: Asked 'Any HSA distributions in 2025', the filer thinks nothing was taken out and answers no. Part II is then skipped, so line 15 is never asked even though the beneficiary paid the decedent's medical bills.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: 'the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death... On Part II, line 14a, enter the fair market value of the HSA as of the date of death.'
findings.fix: Ask the gate as: 'In 2025 did you or your spouse take money out of an HSA, receive a Form 1099-SA, or become the beneficiary of an HSA of someone who died?'

findings.who: A filer paid medical bills out of pocket in 2023 or 2024, after opening the HSA, and in 2025 withdrew HSA money to reimburse themselves.
findings.why_no: The question asks how much of the money that came out 'paid for medical costs'. The bills were already paid from the filer's own funds, so the 2025 withdrawal seems to have paid no medical costs. The filer may then answer zero or exclude these amounts.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 15: 'distributions from your HSA that were used to pay you for qualified medical expenses not reimbursed by insurance or other coverage and that you incurred after the HSA was established.'
findings.fix: Reword the question as 'paid for, or reimbursed you for, medical costs that count (including costs from earlier years, if incurred after you opened the HSA)', and use the same wording in the gate.

findings.who: A filer whose HSA distributions included an excess contribution withdrawn after the return's due date, and who spent that money on doctor bills.
findings.why_no: The question counts any money that came out and paid for medical costs that count. Nothing in it excludes a late-withdrawn excess contribution, so the filer includes it. This is an overstatement rather than a dropped amount.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 15: 'Do not include the distribution of an excess contribution taken out after the due date, including extensions, of your return even if used for qualified medical expenses.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Do not count a withdrawal of an excess contribution made after your return's due date, even if it paid medical costs.'

locators: p. 8, Line 15

p. 8, Line 15, "Only include on line 15 distributions from your HSA that were used to pay you for qualified medical expenses not reimbursed by insurance or other coverage and that you incurred after the HSA was established" and "Any person who would be a dependent except that"; p. 9, Line 15, TIP, divorced or separated parents; p. 2, Qualified Medical Expenses, "You cannot treat insurance premiums as qualified medical expenses unless the premiums are for:", "Long-term care (LTC) insurance", "Health care continuation coverage (such as coverage under COBRA)" and "Health care coverage while receiving unemployment compensation under federal or state law"; p. 3, "Medicare and other health care coverage if you were 65 or older (other than premiums for a Medicare supplemental policy, such as Medigap)", "Coverage under (2) and (3) can be for your spouse or a dependent meeting the requirement." and "are under age 65, Medicare premiums for your spouse or dependents (who are age 65 or older) are generally not qualified medical expenses"

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly. One spouse has family HDHP coverage at any time in 2025, and each spouse has an HSA of their own, so each needs their own Form 8889 on the joint return.
findings.why_no: The computed gate needs filing status married filing separately, so it is false on any joint return. The spouse's-HSA question is never asked, and the line is forced to false.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules to figure the amount on line 6 ... divide the amount on line 5 equally between you and your spouse, unless you both agree on a different allocation". The rule is not limited to separate returns.
findings.fix: Drop the married-filing-separately condition. Ask about separate HSAs whenever the filer is married at the end of 2025 and treated as having family HDHP coverage. On a joint return, ask whether each spouse had an HSA, then apply the Line 6 allocation (or the refusal) to both spouses' Forms 8889, unless the joint path already handles this allocation elsewhere.

findings.who: A married filer filing separately who has self-only HDHP coverage through their own employer. The filer's spouse has family HDHP coverage through the spouse's job, and the spouse also has an HSA.
findings.why_no: The filer reads "treated as having family HDHP coverage" as asking about their own plan, which is self-only. They answer no, not knowing the rule that a spouse's family coverage is treated as family coverage for both spouses.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"; "If you are treated as having family coverage for each month ..."
findings.fix: Ask facts the filer can check: "Did you or your husband or wife have family (not self-only) HDHP coverage at any time in 2025?" Then compute "treated as having family coverage" from the answer, applying the spouse rule in the tool.

findings.who: A married filer filing separately who reads the gated question's preface "For this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return)".
findings.why_no: The joint-return preface on a separate return can make the filer unsure whose HSA is asked about, or think the question applies only to joint returns. They may answer no about their own HSA, or skip the question.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"
findings.fix: On a separate return, drop the joint-return preface and ask: "Did your husband or wife (who files their own return) have an HSA of their own at any time in 2025, or was anything put into one for 2025?"

locators: p. 7, Line 6, "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"
p. 7, Line 6, "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules to figure the amount on line 6"

p. 7, Line 6, "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules to figure the amount on line 6" and "divide the amount on line 5 equally between you and your spouse, unless you both agree on a different allocation"

findings.who: A filer moved an IRA distribution into an HSA as a qualified HSA funding distribution in February 2025. They became disabled in September 2025, left their job, and lost HDHP coverage on October 1, 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about a testing period that began in 2024. This filer's testing period began in 2025, so the truthful answer is no. The tool then never asks the disability question, even though the failure, and any income from it, falls in 2025.
findings.line: f8889.disabled_if_failed (and through it Form 8889 line 19 and the 10% additional tax)
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Testing period: "The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA ... If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to cover a qualified HSA funding distribution contributed in 2024 or in 2025 whose testing period was failed during 2025. Ask the disability question for that case too.

findings.who: A filer was first HDHP-covered on December 1, 2024. A preparer or software took the full-year 2024 HSA contribution limit for them. They lost HDHP coverage in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether "the last-month rule was used for 2024". The filer does not know that legal label and never chose it knowingly, so they answer no. The failure is then dropped and the disability question is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2, Last-month rule: "You may consider yourself an 'eligible individual' for the entire year if you are an eligible individual on the 1st day of the last month of the tax year ... You are then subject to a 'testing period'."
findings.fix: Ask facts the filer can check instead: the months of HDHP coverage in 2024, and whether the 2024 HSA contribution was more than the months covered would allow (or whether the 2024 Form 8889 line 3 used the full-year amount). Classify the last-month rule from those answers.

findings.who: A filer became disabled in 2025, applied for disability benefits, and enrolled in Medicare because of the disability. That enrollment ended their HSA eligibility within the testing period.
findings.why_no: The help says "Losing it for any other reason, such as Medicare at 65 ... means No." The filer sees that Medicare is what ended eligibility and answers no, though the underlying cause was becoming disabled.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2, Testing period: "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include in income ..."
findings.fix: Change the help to: "Answer Yes if becoming disabled is why you lost HDHP-only coverage, including Medicare you enrolled in because of the disability. Answer No for Medicare at 65 or a job change unrelated to a disability."

findings.who: A filer became disabled in 2025, could no longer work, lost their employer's HDHP, and moved to a spouse's non-HDHP plan. They still hold the HSA and continue to take distributions from it.
findings.why_no: The question says "stop being able to have an HSA". The filer still has the account, which the instructions confirm they may keep using, so they answer no. The help also names "a new job's ordinary health plan" as a No, and the filer may read their move to the spouse's plan that way.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2: "You can receive distributions from an HSA even if you are not currently eligible to have contributions made to the HSA." Same page, Testing period: "other than because of death or becoming disabled".
findings.fix: Reword to: "Did you stop being eligible to contribute to an HSA (lose HDHP-only coverage) during the testing period because you became disabled, including coverage changes that followed from the disability?"

locators: p. 2, Testing period, "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include in income the total contributions made that would not have been made except for the last-month rule"; p. 8, Testing period, "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income"
p. 2, Testing period; p. 8, Testing period
